Docs / Data fetching / Caching

Caching HTTP responses

Caching lets a browser or a CDN reuse a response it has already downloaded instead of asking your server again. A good caching policy makes pages load faster, cuts bandwidth costs and keeps your origin server calm during traffic spikes. This guide explains the headers that control caching and shows the policies that work for most apps.

The Cache-Control header

Every caching decision starts with the Cache-Control response header. The most important directive is max-age, which tells caches how many seconds a response stays fresh. While a response is fresh, the browser uses it without contacting the server at all.

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

The example above is the right policy for fingerprinted assets such as app.3f9a1c.js, whose file name changes whenever their content changes. One year is the conventional maximum, and the immutable directive tells browsers not to revalidate the file even when the user reloads the page.

Note: never send a long max-age for HTML documents or for URLs that keep the same name after a deploy, because users will keep seeing the old version until the cache expires.

no-cache is not no-store

The names are confusing, so it is worth being precise. The no-cache directive allows a cache to store the response, but it must check with the server before every reuse. The no-store directive forbids storing the response anywhere, which is what you want for pages that contain private data such as account balances.

DirectiveStores a copyRevalidates before use
max-age=600YesAfter 10 minutes
no-cacheYesEvery time
no-storeNoNot applicable

Validators and 304 responses

When a cached response becomes stale, the browser does not have to download it again. If the response carried an ETag or a Last-Modified header, the browser sends a conditional request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since. If nothing changed, the server answers with a short 304 Not Modified response and the browser keeps using its copy.

GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "a1b2c3"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

Revalidation still costs a round trip, but it saves the transfer of the body. For large JSON payloads that rarely change, this can cut bandwidth by more than 90 percent.

Serving stale content while revalidating

The stale-while-revalidate extension lets a cache serve a stale response immediately while it fetches a fresh one in the background. Users get an instant page, and the next visitor gets updated content. It works best for data that can be a few seconds or minutes out of date, such as product listings or blog indexes.

Caching personalized responses

Shared caches such as CDNs must never mix up responses meant for different users. Mark personalized responses with private, and use the Vary header when the same URL returns different content depending on a request header such as Accept-Language. Avoid Vary: Cookie on public pages, because it effectively disables shared caching.

Recommended defaults

  • Fingerprinted static assets: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
  • HTML pages: no-cache with an ETag.
  • Public API responses: a short max-age plus stale-while-revalidate.
  • Private data: private, no-store.
